In 2008, Jamie Dimon's team ran risk check ins 5 times a day.
In 2026, AI agents run them continuously on every borrower. All at once.

That gap is the biggest story in banking right now.

Dimon's fortress balance sheet kept JPMorgan standing while Bear Stearns and Lehman disappeared. His lesson has stayed with me my entire career: PREPARATION BEATS PREDICTION.

But the fortress of 2008 was built by humans, for human-speed risk. Here's what AI just changed:

- AI now reads and spreads bank & financial statements in minutes, with verification agents checking every number against its source
- Agentic underwriting moved from pilots to production loan files, with finance teams adopting it up ~600% in one year
- Credit decisions that took weeks now take hours while AI monitors the portfolio 24/7 instead of once a year

And yet most banks are still trying to bolt AI onto ten disconnected tools, with an analyst as the integration layer. 

That's not a fortress. That's a fax machine with a chatbot.

The institutions that win this decade will run what I call the AI Credit Operating System: one platform where AI agents handle intake, spreading, credit memos, portfolio monitoring, etc. feeding a business credit score built on financial statements, bank data and every signal in between.

Models matter. Data matters more.

I'm making the full argument on stage at Ai4 - Artificial Intelligence Conferences Las Vegas - the largest AI industry event.

📍 Aug 6 · 11:30 AM · The Venetian, Las Vegas

If you lead credit, risk or AI at a bank or fintech, come find me there. And if you haven't registered yet, DM me for a discount code.

A Chief Credit Officer told me she'd been using Moody's CreditLens for 8 years. Then she told me what she actually thought of it. I was doing customer discovery. 18 months before Accend had our underwriting product.

I sat across from this CCO at a mid-sized regional bank (people are nice - she invited me to their office based on just a cold DM and my curiosity to build something in this underserved space). This is someone with 20 years in commercial credit, well-regarded in her market, the kind of person who had seen multiple generations of fintech come and go.

I asked her: "Can you walk me through your underwriting and spreading process?"

She pointed to Moody's CreditLens on her screen.

"We use this," she said. "We've used it for eight years."

I asked: "Do you like it?" (I already knew she's gonna say no hah!)

There was a pause.

"I like that it exists," she said. "I do not like using it."

Then she walked me through it. The upload workflow. The manual field correction. The triage before uploading to Moody's so they don't overcharge her. The fact that her team had built a parallel Excel process alongside it because CreditLens' output wasn't formatted the way their credit policy required. The fact that every update from Moody's (rare!) broke something her team had configured, and nobody from Moody's called to warn them.

"We spend about 40% of our time managing the tool," she said. "Not using it. Managing it."

I thought about that number for months.

There are roughly 4,500 community and regional banks in the US. If the average credit team is spending 40% of its time managing its underwiting/spreading tool rather than the actual work - that's not just a market opportunity. That's an indictment of an entire product category.

The incumbents won through relationships, not through product quality. They stayed because switching felt too hard, not because anyone loved them.

We built Accend to be the thing people actually want to use. Not the thing they use because there's nothing better. The proof is in what happens when a bank does switch: their analysts notice it within a week. The feedback we get most often isn't just "this is more accurate." It's "I actually don't dread this process anymore."

That's the bar we set for ourselves after that conversation.

Make the work feel like work (read: fun) again, not like managing a tool.

Most founders at YC pivot away from their original idea. Three weeks into the batch, I realized I needed to pivot toward a problem I'd been sitting next to for three years and hadn't fully faced.

When I joined the S23 batch, Accend was a different company: reasonable idea, good team, and a thesis about where B2B fintech was heading. In the first three weeks I kept getting the same feedback from partners and founders: "Who is the customer and what do they feel when the problem is solved?" I couldn't answer that cleanly. At YC, if you can't, you need to find the problem where you can.

I kept coming back to something I had seen at Brex. A workflow I'd watched dozens of times but never fully interrogated: the commercial underwriting process. Analysts retyping numbers from PDFs into spreadsheets into systems that don't talk to each other, writing credit memos from scratch every time, manually calculating ratios they don't fully trust. Tasks that belonged in 2003, not 2025. I knew the workflow intimately, had built products around it, talked to the credit leaders who ran it. The pain was real, the stakes were high, and the incumbents like Moody's hadn't meaningfully innovated in years.

YC helped me see one thing more clearly: when this problem is solved, the customer feels like they got their team back. Analysts finally doing the work they were hired to do: judgment, relationships, decisions, instead of spending Tuesday retyping balance sheets. That's a powerful feeling to give someone.

So we pivoted, went deep on financial spreading and AI-powered underwriting automation, and started calling CCOs and credit teams. Within six months of the batch, Brex was our customer. Within a year, a large S&P 500 company displaced Moody's to sign with us at Accend.

The lesson I took from all of it: the best problems are the ones you've already lived inside of, you just have to stop looking for something new and turn around.

I have a bad habit 🤐 
Whenever I hear something repeated too many times, I start assuming it’s wrong.

Lately, it’s been: “Lending is slowing.”

So I went and looked at the data…turns out, banks forgot to slow down.
Balance sheets are still sitting near highs. Loans are still going out the door.

Which raises a more interesting question:
If lending isn’t slowing then why does it feel so hard right now?

My take: Deals didn’t disappear. They just got… heavier.
- More docs
- More edge cases
- More scrutiny
- More “wait, can we double-check this?”

Same demand. Same capital. MORE FRICTION. 
So the real constraint isn’t money. It’s this weird, invisible thing:
👉 how fast you can trust your own underwriting

The lenders who win won’t look dramatically different.
They’ll just quietly move faster, break less, and trust their numbers sooner
It’s a small shift.

But those are usually the ones that compound. Seeing this pattern a lot at Accend.

Curious: does it feel like lending slowed where you sit, or just… got harder?

Everyone assumes the largest banks in the US will dominate AI in lending since they have the data, the budgets, the engineering teams. But I think they'll lose this race to banks a fraction of their size. Here's why:

The largest institutions have a structural problem that doesn't get talked about enough: decades of overlapping loan origination systems, multiple cores from acquisitions, credit policies that take months and multiple committees to amend, and risk functions whose entire careers were built on the workflows AI is about to make obsolete. The technology change is possible, the organizational change is nearly impossible.

A $4B bank doesn't have any of that. One LOS, a Chief Credit Officer who answers to the board, and a competitive imperative to do more with less because they can't out-hire the largest institutions for talent. Every time I walk into one of these banks, the conversation goes from "interesting" to "when can we start" in 30 minutes. At the largest institutions it goes to procurement, then security review, then a pilot in one region, then a steering committee.

This same dynamic played out in the early 2010s with digital banking. Everyone assumed the largest banks would dominate. Instead a generation of regional banks leapfrogged them by skipping straight to mobile-first.

The community and regional banks that move in the next 18 months will be writing loans faster, with better credit quality, than institutions 50 times their size. Some of them will use that advantage to grow into the gap the largest banks can't fill because they can't move fast enough.

The story of the next lending cycle is being written at the regionals right now. This is exactly why we built Accend - for banks that want to move fast without ripping out their existing systems.

Curious if others are seeing this too. What's your read on where community and regional banks stand on AI adoption right now?

Most commercial credit losses don't happen because the underwriting was wrong. They happen because the covenant monitoring was wrong and nobody caught it in time.

Here's how it works at most banks today: A loan closes with 14 covenants, financial ratios the borrower must maintain, reporting deadlines they must hit, restrictions on what they can do without consent. The borrower submits quarterly compliance certificates, sometimes they do, sometimes they don't, and sometimes they do but nobody reads them carefully.

Eighteen months later the loan is in trouble. Someone pulls the file and discovers the borrower tripped a debt service coverage covenant four quarters ago and nobody caught it. By the time anyone noticed, the early warning signal had already become a workout situation.

The loss didn't happen because the underwriting was wrong. It happened because the monitoring was wrong and by the time anyone looked up, the optionality to act early was gone.

Most banks have no real-time view of covenant compliance across their portfolio, just a stack of compliance certificates and an annual review process that catches problems 9-15 months after they start. Accend for Banking does exactly this -- pulling financials as they're submitted, automatically running scheduled covenant tests, flagging trips the day they happen, and surfacing overdue items before they become workout situations. It converts that quarterly rearview mirror into a live dashboard and changes the entire posture of the credit function from reactive to proactive.

Every credit officer I've shown this to has the same reaction: "this should already exist." The banks that get there first will have a portfolio quality advantage that compounds for a decade.

I had a conversation last month with the CFO of a mid-market manufacturing company who had just refinanced a $40M credit facility. I asked him how he picked his lender and his answer changed how I think about competitive dynamics in commercial banking.

"The pricing was within 15 basis points across all four banks. I picked the one that closed in 23 days instead of 90."

Four times faster, across a $40M decision. Same price, different speed, different winner. This is the part of the AI-in-banking conversation that gets lost. The industry talks endlessly about cost reduction, efficiency ratios, FTE savings, and those are real, but they are table stakes. The actual prize is on the revenue side and almost nobody is talking about it.

When you compress underwriting turnaround from 90 days to 20 days, you become a fundamentally different product. When you compress it to same-day, you become a different category entirely. You win deals you would have lost on speed alone, serve borrowers your competitors can't reach, and charge a premium for certainty, because to a CFO trying to close an acquisition or fund a working capital gap, getting an answer today is worth considerably more than 15 basis points.

That's what we're building at Accend. The work that consumes most of those 90 days, gathering documents, spreading financials, calculating ratios, drafting the credit memo, turned around the same day with expert validation built in. The credit officer spends their time on the judgment that moves the deal forward. The borrower gets an answer in days, not a quarter.

The banks that get there first will pull share from the ones that don't, even at higher rates, because pricing power follows speed. If you are a Chief Credit Officer reading this, the question worth asking is how much AI can win you, not just how much it can save you. Those are different questions and the second one has a much bigger number at the end.
